o: Delete exactly one character so every remaining letter occurs equally often. With |word| ≤ 100, brute force is trivially fast: build a frequency map, try decrementing each distinct letter's count, and check whether all nonzero counts are equal. "abcc" → drop one 'c' gives {a:1,b:1,c:1} → true. "aazz" → dropping anything leaves counts {1,2} → false. The constraints mean even an O(26·n) approach is overkill-safe, so correctness clarity beats micro-optimization.
k: Only distinct letters matter — at most 26 trials.
After a trial deletion, all nonzero frequencies must be identical.
Must delete exactly one character; empty result never occurs since |word| ≥ 2.

a.i: For each index, rebuild counts without that character and test equality of all nonzero counts. O(n²) but n ≤ 100.
s: For each index i, count letters skipping i.
If all nonzero counts equal, return true.
a.t: O(n²) — n trials, each O(n) counting

a.i: Removing any occurrence of the same letter yields identical counts, so only ≤ 26 trials are needed: build the Counter once, temporarily decrement each distinct letter, and validate.
s: For each distinct letter, decrement its count, collect nonzero values, check they're all equal, restore.
Return true if any trial passes.
a.t: O(n + 26²) — one count pass plus constant trials

w: Prefer Approach 2 — it shows you noticed occurrences of the same letter are interchangeable. Common pitfall: forgetting that deleting a letter whose count becomes 0 removes it from consideration entirely (handled by filtering v > 0). Edge cases: two-letter words like "aa" (true, drop one) and words like "aabbcc" (false — must delete exactly one). Follow-up: allow deleting zero or one character?
